Who can sanction prosecution for undervaluing a document and

can it be withdrawn and if so under what circumstances?

Collectors, Divisional Officers and District Registrars are authorised to

sanction prosecutions for offences under the Stamp Act (vide Sec. 70

and Note thereunder.) The following are also authorized.

(1) Inspector General R & S, (2) Assistant Inspector General (R &
S), (3) Deputy Inspector General (R. & S) and (4) Assistant District
Registrars.

All the above officers can also stay or withdraw such prosecutions if the

offence is compounded and after composition fee is collected. Sub-

Registrars, Grade-I who-are authorised to exercise powers of District

Registrar under Section 35, Registration Act can only compound offences.

Can a District Registrar sanction prosecutions for offences under

Stamp Law. Can he compound the offences or stay or withdraw

prosecutions?

District Registrar can sanction prosecutions for offences under Stamp
Law, stay or withdraw such prosecutions and compound offences (Vide
Note under Sec. 70 APSM)

Can a person be prosecucted for failure to pay the penalty and if
so, under what circumstances?

The effect of sections 43 and 62 is to authorise prosecutions under Sec.70
for non-payment of penalty whether or not, intention to defraud
Government of its revenue is made out (Note-2 under Section 62 APSM).
Intention to defraud the Government from its legitimate revenue need
not be established except in cases falling under secs. 64 and 65(b)
Mention the cases in which an intent to defraud the Government
is required to be shown for instituting a prosecution and the cases
where such an intention is not a necessary element of the offence?
Intention to defraud the Government of its revenue is required to be
established in cases falling under Sec. 64 and 65(b). It is not necessary in
other cases. (See also S.No. 20 infra).

Editor’s Note:

Unstamped receipts and promotes are governed by separate provisions of
the Stamp Act (Vide Sec.34)

Stamp Duty on instruments has to be paid before or at the time of their
execution (Sec. 17 ). Where documents are required to be produced in offices
or Courts immediately, the scope for evasion of duty is less (Sec. 33). But in
other cases there is a tendency to evade the duty. Parties are inclined to take
the risk as the chances of detection are remote. Hence a system of levy of
penalty not exceeding 10 times deficit duty is laid down to deter the parties
from taking the risk. If a deficitly stamped document is produced in evidence
the court will have to levy penalty equal to 10 times the deficit duty though the
Collector has power to remit a part of it later. In other cases the Collector can
levy penalty not exceedirig 10 times the deficit duty by a judicious use of these
powers the tendency to evade payment of duty at the proper time can be curbed.

Amore common method of evading duty is by undervaluation of instruments
intentionally. Such an act contravenes Sec. 27 punishable under Sec. 64. But it
is very difficult to prove intention to defraud Government which is essential to
secure prosecution. The introduction of Sec. 47A curbed this tendency to some
extent. But even under this scheme correct particulars of buildings are being
suppressed to evade payment of proper duty. Intensive spot and post facto
inspections and prosecution of parties involved in the offence is a positive
measure to curb this tendency.

20. State briefly the provisions of the Act for the prevention of
undervaluation of properties?

Sec. 27 says that all facts and circumstances affecting the chargeability
of instruments to duty shall be fully and truly set forth. Sec. 64 lays down
that if any person contravenes the provisions of Sec. 27 with an intention
to defraud Government of its revenue, he is punishable with fine upto Rs.
5,000/- in addition to deficit duty (Sec. 64-A.). But it is difficult to prove
such intention in a court of law. There is also no method of ascertaining
real consideration in respect of sale deeds. So Sec. 47-A was introduced
and consequential amendments were made to Sch. I-A. The duty in
respect of sales is made payable on consideration or market value of the
property whichever is higher. In respect of Gift, Exchange, Partition,
Settlement and release the duty is payable on market value of property.
Guidelines were provided to Registering officers to calculate market value.
If the value declared in the document is less than such market value, the
Registering Officer, before registering the document has to refer the
case to the Collector under Section 47A who determines the correct
Classified Topics 287

21.

22.

23.

24,

market value and collects the difference of duty if any. If the party is
aggrieved he may move the civil court.(See 47-A sub section (4) and
(5)) (Chapter 10 (2) MV Scheme supra)

This provision can plug leakage of stamp revenue if the Collectors
promptly dispose of references under Sec. 47-A after proper enquiry
and if tendency to suppress correct particulars of buildings in Annexure
I-A_ is checked by intensive spot inspections and post facto inspections
immediately after registration of such instruments
What is the prerequisite that should be fulfilled before an offence
under the Act can be prosecuted ?

The District Collector or any officer appointed as Collector under Sec.
70 of the Stamp Act should sanction prosecution before prosecution is
commenced. (Sec. 70).

(v). PROPER OFFICER

Who are the officers appointed as " Proper Officers "" under the

Act in A.P and what are their functions

The officers mentioned in Appendix-| to the Indian Stamp Rules 1925

(Vide Chapter IC Supra) are appointed as "Proper Officers" They are

empowered to affix and impress or perforate labels on unexecuted

instruments. They are called " Proper Officers "

What precautions should a Proper Officer take while affixing

impressing and cancelling labels ?

(a) He should see that the document was not already executed. (Rule
11)

(b) The document mentioned in Atpendix-II and I] alone can be affixed
with impressed labels (Rule 10) (Notification appended to
G.O.Ms.No. 92, Rev. dated 16.9.1967)

(c) Heshould impress or perforate the labels with a machine. He should
stamp or write on the face of labels the date of Stamping.(Rule
11(1).)

(d) Where the duty amounts to Rs. 5/- and below Rs. 20/- he should
affix his initials on the face of the labels, where the duty amounts
to Rs. 20 or more he shall affix his signature immediately under the
labels (Rule 11(2).)

(vi). REFUNDS

What are the rules governing refund of spoiled Stamps? When
can refund be made without deduction?

Sec. 49 governs the refund of spoiled stamps Sec. 49(a) & (b) relate to
288 Classified Topics

25.

Stamps spoiled before execution of the documents Sec. 49(c) relates to
refund of Stamps used for Bills of Exchange and pronote and Sec. 49(d)
relates to refund of spoiled stamps used for executed documents. The
Rules governing refund are as follows:

The Collector may require any person claiming refund or his agent to
make an oral deposition or to file an affidavit setting forth the
circumstances under which the claim has arisen. The Collector may also
call for evidence of witness — (Rule 19)

When an order is passed by the Collector sanctioning the allowance or
calling for further evidence, then if the allowance is not taken or if the
required evidence is not furnished within one year, the application shall
be struck off and the spoiled stamps sent to the Inspector General of
Registration and Stamps for destruction. (Vide Rule 20).

Deduction need not be made when other stamps are issued in lieu of
spoiled stamps. (Vide Note-2 under Sec. 53 APSM)

What relief is afforded in regard to the following?
(a) spoiled impressed Stamps.
(b) Misused Stamps
(c) Stamps not required for use.
(d) Stamps used in excess of the required value required
Items (a) (b) and (d) :— In the case of spoiled or misused stamps and

Stamps used in excess of the value required and consequently treated as spoiled
or misused stamps under Sec. 52 the following relief is allowed. The Collector
may give in lieu of such Stamps —

(a) other stamps of same description and values or
(b) Stamps of any other description of the same value or

(d) the same value in money deducting 10 paise for each rupee or
fraction of rupee —(Sec. 53.)

Item (c) : — In the case of stamps not required for use, the Collector

shall repay the value of such stamps in money deducting 10 paise for each
rupee or fraction of a rupee -(Vide Sec. 54, BSOS 89 and 90.)

All stamps admitted for refund or renewal and cancelled under the Act

destroyed. The entries in the Registers shall be verified with the Stamps
taken out for destruction by the officer incharge of the local depot and
burnt monthly in the presence of Collector or officer incharge of local
depot if so ordered by the Collector. A Certificate shall be recorded in
the Register by the said officer to the effect that the Stamps were
destroyed by burning in his presence. A copy of the certificate shall be
sent to the Accountant General and to the Inspector General (R & S)

Describe the procedure by which a person in possession of spoiled
stamps and unused stamps can claim refund?

The party for whose use the Stamps were purchased is entitled to claim
refund. He or his duly authorised Agent should apply within the prescribed
time limits (Sec. 50, 52 & 54) to the officer authorised to sanction refunds.
He should give a statement on oath or affirmation or an affidavit setting
forth the circumstances under which the claim arose. If so called for, he
should produce the evidence of witnesses — (Rule 19.) If the refund is
not taken within one year from date of sanction or if the evidence is not
produced within one year the application will be struck off (Rule 20.)

(ix) SECTION 73

Explain in full the scope of Sec. 73 in the matter of preventing
leakage of Stamp Duty?

or
Elucidate the role of the Registration and Stamps Department
under Sec. 73 of the Act to plug leakage of Stamp Revenue?

Sec. 73 empowers the Collector or any person authorised by him to audit
the records in the custody of every public officer to detect fraud or omission
in relation to payment of Stamp Duty. All Revenue Divisional Officers
and P As to Collectors are declared as “Collectors” under the section.
Hence it is the primary responsibility of the Revenue officials to conduct
such an audit. But they are not able to do it in view of their multifarious
duties. In the erstwhile state of Hyderabad, Inspector General of.
Registration and Stamps was entrusted with this duty. (Vide Sec. 69 of
Hyderabad Stamp Act), The system was effective. There were inspecting
officers to assist the Inspector General in this function. After the
introduction -of Indian Stamp Act in the Telangana area, the Inspector
General, R & S was declared as “Collector” under Sec. 73 throughout
the State of Andhra Pradesh and Regional Inspecting Officers (Stamps)
(R.LOs) were appointed in the Districts for conducting audit under Sec.
73. These posts were later converted as Deputy Inspectors General R
& S. The Superintendents working in these offices were also empowered
to conduct audit of the records in Public offices of and below the Taluk /
Mandal level.

The Inspector General R & S, the Deputy Inspector General R & S and
the Superintendents in their offices were declared as Collectors under
296

53

Classified Topics

Sec. 38(2), 40 and 42 to enable them to impound, levy and collect deficit
stamp duties on deficitly stamped documents detected by them in audit.

Editor’s Submission :
The system of audit is not fully effective for the following reasons : -

(1) The Public Offices are many and the Deputy Inspectors General
and Office Superintendents with skeleton staff are unable to cover
all the offices even once in 10 years.

(2) Several Heads of offices audited are not able to pay required
attention to the audit remarks. Some of the officers are not
surrendering the deficitly stamped documents for collection of deficit
duties and penalties.

(3) The documents are generally impounded after several years. The
addresses of parties are not known sufficiently

(4). The duty payable in some cases is generally too low that the cost in
issuing notices to parties by Registered post in such cases is more
than the duty to be realised

(5) The Deputy Inspectors General have been gradually entrusted with
additional powers to control and supervise the work in connection
with the regular administration of several subordinate offices
(Registrars Officers and Sub Registrar’s Offices) in their zone
without adequate increase of staff in the offices. Consequently it
has become practically not possible to pursue “follow up” action
on their audit remarks involving loss of Stamp Revenues due to the
state and continue audit of the records in Public Offices periodically
and at frequent intervals.

(6) The only advantage is that officers are enlightened to some extent
about the duty payable on documents generally produced before
them and they prevent future leakage.

(x) SUPPLEMENTAL DEEDS

Mention all the instruments under Schedule I-A in connection
with which supplemental deed can be employed?

Supplemental deeds can be employed in respect of only Sales, mortgages
and settlements - (Vide Sec. 4.)

(a) Name two instruments that fall under the term “supplemental
deed”?

(1) Ratification deed executed by a party after attaining majority during
whose minority the property was sold by his guardian.

(2) Ratification deed executed by a co-owner to a sale deed executed
by the other co-owners.

In both the cases there should be no further consideration.

What are the special provisions made in respect of several
instruments employed for completing a transactions?

Where in the case of Sale, Mortgage or Settlement several instruments
are employed for completing the transaction, the principal instrument
only shall be chargeable with the prescribed duty under Schedule I or I-
A as the case may be and each other instrument shall be chargeable
with a duty of Rs. 5/-(Vide Section 4.) Supplemental deeds do not attract
transfer duty. There shall be no consideration for execution of supp!mental
deeds

(xi) STAMP VENDORS

What are the powers and duties of Sub-Registrar with regard to
licensed Stamp Vendors?

When a party applies to Stamp Vendors for a Stamp paper higher than
the highest value of Stamp which the Vendor is authorised to sell, he
should not attempt to supply such stamp by the sale of a number of
Stamped sheets he is authorised to sell. (Vide Rule 39 (xiv) of the Rules
for supply and distribution of Stamps.) The Sub-Registrar should report
to the District Registrar (licensing authority) any contravention of this
Rule by the licensed Stamp Vendor (vide Note (1) under the said Sub-
Brea.)

Stamp Vendors are strictly prohibited from altering endorsements made
by them on stamped papers. Any Stamp Vendor proved to have
contravened this rule is liable to have his license cancelled — (Vide BSO
TH2\vii)

The Sub-Registrars may receive applications form private parties, Banks
and Corporate bodies for appointment as Stamp Vendors who shall
submit them to the District Registrar after due enquiry for consideration
and orders. (BSO 77(2)(vii)(b))

What are the rules governing the appointment and dismissal of
Stamp Vendors and to whom does an appeal lie?

Private parties, Commercial Banks and Corporate Bodies can be licensed
as Stamp Vendors. In the twin cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad
and elsewhere, the District Registrars concerned are empowered to grant
licences to private parties etc.,to sell Stamps. Applications for licences
should be stamped with rupee one under Court Fee Act.

They must give an engagement bond in the prescribed form and the
licence will be issued in the prescribed form (vide Chapter 12 infra).
They should sell the stamps at the place shown in the licence from 10
A.M. to 5 P.M. on all working days except Sundays. They should not
write documents for parties. They are allowed discount of 2.2% on Non-
Judicial, Hundi and copy stamps and 1% on Court Fee Stamps(vide
Chapter 12 infra for revised rates of commission from 2006). He must
write the prescribed endorsements on the stamps sold by him and maintain
sale and stock registers. They should always maintain sufficient stock of
Stamps and sell them only at face value. They can sell stamps on sundays
and other holidays (BSO 80) .

What are the duties of Ex-offico Stamp Vendors? Enumerate the
rules framed under the Act regarding sale of Stamps by Ex-officio
Vendors?

They should sell only such stamps as they may be authorised to sell by
the CCRA or Government.

They should make on each stamp sold to a person other than Stamp
Vendor the endorsements prescribed in Rule 30(2) (vide S.No.60 above)
and make corresponding entries in the sales register

They should sell stamps on demand to any party on tendering value.
Obsolete stamps should not be sold.

They should maintain the accounts prescribed by the Board (C.C.R.A)
and Government and allow their inspection by the Collector or other
Officer authorised by him or by the CCRA or Government.

They should deliver up the stock on demand by the Collector or other
Officer authorised by the, CCRA or Government.

They should try to issue a single sheet of the required value and if it
is not available, fewest possible number of sheets should be issued to
make up the value.

When the demand is for a stamp higher than the highest value, the vendor
is authorised to sell, he should not try to sell such stamp by issuing a
number of stamps he is authorised to sell. (vide Rule 30 of the Rules for
the Supply and distribution of Stamps).

(xii). SALE IN FAVOUR OF MORTGAGEE

67. What are the conditions to be fulfilled for a party to be entitled to
deduct Stamp Duty paid in respect of a mortgage from the Stamp
Duty payable on a transfer (sale) with reference to the second
proviso to Section 24?
The following conditions have to be fulfilled.

(i) The mortgage should be extinguished.

(ii) The sale must be by the mortgagor or his heirs or legal representatives or

"a person who acquired the right on the mortgaged property from the

mortgagor by way of transfer of mortgage.

(iii) The sale must be in favour of the mortgagee or his successor or to a
person to whom the mortgage is transferred.

(iv) Whole or part of the property subject to mortgage should be transferred.
(Vide Notes 2 and 3 under Sec. 24 APSM.)

(v) If only part of the mortgaged property is sold other property should not
be included.

68. Examine and state whether the concession under proviso to Sec.
24 is applicable in the following cases?

(1) ‘A’ mortgaged his property to ‘B’ and ‘B’ transferred his mortgage
right to ‘C’. ‘A’ now sells the property to ‘C’.
The concession applies (Vide Note 2, under Section 24 APSM)

(2) ‘A? mortgaged two items of property to ‘B’ for Rs. 3,000/- ‘A’
now sells one of these items to ‘B’ together with another item
(not included in the mortgage) for Rs. 3,000/- in full discharge of
the debt.
The Concession will not apply if part of the mortgaged property and
other property is sold.

(3) ‘A’ mortgaged 2 items of property to ‘B’ for Rs. 2,000. He now
sells one of these items to ‘B’ in discharge of the entire debt of
Rs. 2,000/- and a cash consideration of Rs. 1,000/-
The concession will apply if part of mortgaged property is sold (Note 3
under Sec. 24APSM).
Classified Topics 303

(4)

‘A’ mortgaged his property to ‘B’. ‘A’ then sold it to ‘C’ on
condition that he should discharge the debt to ‘B’. In the
meanwhile ‘B’ died bequeathing his mortgage rights to his son
‘D’.‘C’ now sells a portion of the property to ‘D’ in full discharge
of the debt.

The concession will apply as the transferor and transferee succeeded to
the rights of the original mortgagor and mortgagee and even if a part of
property is sold (Notes 2 & 3 under Sec. 24.APSM)

(xiii) VALUATIONS

69. How are valuations made and duty calculated in the following cases?

70.

71.

(a) Where value in instrument is expressed in dollars.

(b) Where instrument relates to marketable securities.

(c) Where consideration is annuity payable for a period of SO years.
ANSWERS:

(a) Where the value is expressed in Dollars, the duty shall be calculated
on the value of the dollars in Indian currency according to the
current rate of exchange as on the date of the instrument (Sec.
20).

(b) When the instrument relates to markatable securites the duty shall
be calculated on the value of the said securities according to their
average price on the date of the instrument (Sec. 21).

(c) Where the consideration is annuity for 50 years the duty should be
calculated on the total amount to be paid in 50 years. {Sec. 25(a)}.

How is stamp duty assessed when the value is indeterminate

(i) | When the value is indeterminate in respect of documents chargeable
with advalorem duty, nothing shall be claimable under such
instrument more than the highest amount or value for which, if
stated in the instrument of same description, the Stamp actually
used would, at the time of execution, have been sufficient.

(ii) However, in the case of mining leases, the following procedure
should be adopted if a share of produce or royalty is payable. If
Government is lessor, the Collector shall estimate the royalty. If
private party is lessor the royalty should be taken as Rs. 20,000/- If
the duty is paid on such amount, the entire royalty or share of
produce can be claimed under such lease. (Sec. 26).

Mention two cases in which duty may be paid otherwise than by
stamps?

1.

The unstamped document may be presented to a Collector or other
authorised officer for adjudication under Sec, 31 within one month
from date of execution and the duty determined may be paid in
cash. The Collector or such other officer as the case may be will
add a certificate on the document under Sec, 32 regarding payment
of duty.

The unstamped document may be presented to a collector or other
authorised officer with an offer to pay the duty under Sec, 41 within
one year from date of execution and if such officer is satisfied that
the omission to stamp was occasioned by accident, mistake or urgent
necessity he will accept cash or challan as the case may be and
add a certificate on the document under Sec, 42 regarding payment
of duty.

What are the various safeguards provided in the Act to ensure
payment of the duty at proper time?
Sec. 35 says that if an insufficiently stamped document is produced in
evidence, the Court shall levy deficit duty and penalty equal to 10 times
deficit duty. In respect of other deficitly stamped documents filed before
Public Officers they will be impounded and sent to the collector or other
authorised officer who will levy the deficit duty and penalty not exceeding
10 times the deficit duty under Sec. 40. This is a deterrent against execution
of deficitly stamped documents and non payment of duty at the proper
time.

(i) Sec. 13 lays down that when any document is written on Stamp
papers, the document shall appear on the face of the document
and in such manner that it can not be used for or applied to any
other instrument.

(ii) Rule 7 says that a part of the document shall appear on the face of
each stamp papaer

ii) Rule 11 lays down that the impressed labels can be affixed on the
document by the "Proper Officer" ‘only before execution i.e before
the executant affixes his signature to the document.

(iv) Sec. 17 prescribes that stamp duty shall be paid on the document
before or at the time of its execution. These measures prevent
stamping of documents after execution subject to the provisions of
Section 10A

What are the remedies provided in the Act for the parties to seek

redress against the excessive levy of duty?

The party may appeal to the CCRA under Sec. 56 or may approach the

High Court with a prayer to direct the CCRA to refer the case to it under

Sec. 57. After payment of the duty the party can appeal to the Collector

under Sec. 45 for the refund of the excess duty.

According to Rule 3(iii) of the Stamp Rules 1925 Stamps purchased in
Andhra Pradesh alone shall be used for documents chargeable with duty
under the Article as in force in Andhra Pradesh. This measure prevents
leakage of Stamp Revenue to other states.

Which is the authority empowered to examine and impound
unstamped sale deed? Can a village officer or a Revenue
Inspector impound a sale deed?

Every person having authority to receive evidence and every person in
charge of public office except an officer of Police can impound an
unstamped sale deed provided it is produced in evidence or in performance
of the duties of such officer (Section 33).

Village Officer (not acting as Village Court) and Revenue Inspector are
not persons incharge of public office and they cannot themselves impound
the documents (Note 3 under Section 33 APSM).
Explain the provisions of the Act designed to eliminate the
possibility of Stamps used for an instrument being used for another
instrument?
(1) Adhesive Stamps : They should be cancelled in such a way that
they cannot be used again. Otherwise the document will be deemed as
unstamped. (Section 12).
(2) Impressed Stamp papers: The instrument shall be written in such
amanner that the Stamp appears on the face of the instrument and
cannot be used for or applied to any other instrument (Sec. 13).
‘When two or more stamped papers or sheets are used for a document,
a portion of the document shall be written on each such stamped paper
or sheet (Rule 7). Otherwise the document shall be deemed as not duly
stamped. (Sec. 15).
(3) Impressed Labels : The Proper Officer only in the case of
unexecuted documents shall impress or perforate the labels and write
on the face of labels the date of impressing or perforating the
same. He should also affix his initials or signatures on the said labels
(Rule 11). This prevents the use of stamps for other documents.

officer?

amount of duty with which any instrument is chargeable he may draw up
a statement of case and refer it to the CCRA {Sec. 56(2)}. The

In what cases can a person paying duty and penalty in respect of

Where duty or penalty was paid under Sec. 35, 37, 40 or 41 by any
person in respect of an instrument, and by agreement or under Section
29 or any other Act for the time being in force some other person was
compelled to bear the duty, the person who actually paid them shall be
entitled to recover the same from the person who is liable to pay the duty
— (Vide Section 44.)

What are the provisions of the Act regarding stamping of
documents executed out of India?

Document other than Bills of Exchange and Pro-notes : The
documents should be stamped within 3 months after they-are received in
India. (Sec. 18(1)). If the nature of the document is such that the party
cannot himself stamp the document he should file it before the Collector
or any other authorised officer for stamping within the said time {Sec.
18(2)} who shall unless he is himself the Proper officer, send the document
and the amount to the proper officc who shall stamp the document with
impressed labels arid return it to the officer from where it was received
for delivery to the party - (Rule 12(2).)

Bills of Exchange and Pronotes : The first holder in India of any Bill
of Exchange payable otherwise than on demand or pronote shall, before
he presents the same for acceptance, payment or endorses, transfers or
otherwise negotiates the same in India affix to it the proper stamps and
cancel it. (Sec. 19).

CHAPTER -7
General Topics

NB: In this Chapter

(i) ‘Sec’ or 'Section' quoted herein relates to Section of the Indian Stamp
Act,1899.

(ii) ‘Art’ or ‘Article’ quoted herein relates to Article of Schedule 1A to the
Stamp Act unless otherwise stated

(iii) 'APSM' denotes Andhra Pradesh Stamp Manual, 1974
(iv) "CCRA' denotes Chief Controlling Revenue Authority
v) "Rule" quoted herein relates to Indian Stamp Rules, 1925.

1. What is meant by the term “Stamp duty is payable on instrument
but not on transaction”?

OR

Stamp duty is on the instrument as it stands but not on the
transaction. Explain?

Section 3 of the Stamp Act prescribes Stamp duty on the instruments
listed out in the Schedules I and IA to the Act but not on transaction. So
the thing which is made liable to duty is the instrument but not the
transaction.

If a contract of purchase and sale can be, or is, carried out without an
instrument, the case is not within the section and no duty need be paid.
If anyone can carry on the transaction without an instrument then the
Stamp law does not apply to it. If, after entering into contract for sale,
the parties, in spite of the risk involved, refrain from getting the actual
deed of sale prepared, they can successfully evade payment of duty.
The Actis not intended to fetter the proceedings of the parties, and if
a party acts in a way as not to be hit, he has a right to do so.

Example .. (i) Goodwill can be conveyed without an instrument. If the
parties prefer not to execute a regular deed of conveyance no duty is
chargeable. Similarly the party can adopt any particular form of
transaction to minimise the duty as it is the instrument that is chargeable
but not transaction.

Example .. (ii) ‘A’ takes a loan of Rs. 5.000/- from B. If no document
is executed, no duty is payable. If he executes a pronote, a less duty is
payable and if he executesabonda slightly higher duty is to be paid
General Topics 317

and if a mortgage is executed it attracts a still higher duty.

However it is to be seen that though the duty is payable on the instrument
but not on the transaction, it is the substance of the transaction as
embodied in the instrument and not the form of the instrument that
determines the duty. It is not the name that is given to the instrument that
determines the duty. A document may be styled as a Release but it may
amount to a conveyance. Hence, though the duty is payable on the
instrument but not on the transaction, regard should be paid to the
substance (but not the form) of the transaction as embodied in the
instrument while determining the duty.

Sections 4 and 5, however, make a departure from this principle. They
take the transaction into consideration in determining the duty but not
the instrument. For example ratification or supplemental deed, mortgage
by conditional sale etc.

2. The Stamp Act is purely a fiscal statute. Its sole object is to increase
and protect State Revenues. Discuss how the efforts of the
Department lead to protection of revenue in effective manner ?
The Registration Department plays a large part in safeguarding the Stamp
Revenue and plug leakages. A majority of the documents chargeable
with duty are registerable and therefore come into the hands of the
Registering officers. They ensure that proper stamp duty is paid on them.
If not, the documents are impounded and deficit duties with penalties
are levied and collected.

The Registering Officer prevents attempts to evade payment of proper
duty by checking suppression of real nature of documents.

The most common method of evasion of payment of proper duty is by
undervaluation of properties and of consideration in sale deeds if
advantageous by suppression of facts and circumstances fully and truly
affecting chargeability of an instrument under stamp Act, (Sec.27). The
department takes action on such undervaluations and contraventions of
Sec.27. The District Registrars and some other officers of the department
are empowered to sanction prosecutions of parties for such
undervaluations (offences). They are also empowered to compound such
offences by leying compounding fee under Sec.70(2). Some Sub-
Registrars of Grade-] and Joint Sub-Registrar I in Registrars Offices
also are empowered to compound such offences. They may enquire into
all cases of undervaluation either suo motu or on receipt of complaints.

The Act was amended inserting Section 47-A with effect from 16-8-

1975 prescribing payment of Stamp duty on market values of the
properties in respect of certain instruments (Act No. XXII of 1971). The
318 General Topics

   

department has compiled market values of properties. All cases where
duties are not paid on such Values are to be promptly referred to
“Collectors” under Sec. 47-A by the Registering Officers for
determination of correct market values.

In these ways the Department is safeguarding the Stamp Revenue in an
effective manner.

3. Examine the justification for prescribing different rates of duty
instead of a uniform rate for the instruments
Stamp duty is a tax imposed by the State on the instruments in order to
raise revenue. There is no quid pro quo. (Something for something). It
has no reference to the services rendered by the State to the tax payer
who pays the duty. Unlike registration fee, which is a fee for services
rendered, stamp duty is a tax and not uniform on all classes of documents.
In respect of certain classes of documents such as Bonds, Conveyances,
Mortgages, Gifts, sales and Settlements etc., the duty is advalorem. In
certain cases like Security Bond, Trust and Award etc., it is advalorem
to a certain extent and thereafter subject to a maximum. In other cases
like adoption deed and affidavit etc., it is a fixed duty. Further in some
cases like conveyances and gifts the rate is higher than on instruments
like, settlement and simple mortgage etc.
In fixing the rates of duty the Legislature obviously took into account
the extent of benefit or nature of right that accrued to the party by means
of the document taxed. For example, in a Gift, the claimant an outsider
(donee may be outsider also), gets absolute rights over the property and
is therefore made to pay a higher duty commensurate with the benefit he
derived. Ina release or in a partition, the claimant has already preexisting
right in the property and hence a less duty is prescribed.
In a Mortgage with possession the mortgagee gets more security for
the recovery of the loan amount than a mortgagee under a simple
mortgage. Again the mortgagee under a simple mortgage is
comparatively safer than one who advances loan under a pronote. Hence
the duty is lesser in the case of a pronote and higher for a simple mortgage
and still higher for a mortgage with possession. The prescription of
uniform rate of duty for all classes of documents will be unscientific.

4, Is it progressive measure to charge conveyance on Market Value
instead of consideration? Give reasons.

OR

The concept of payment of Stamp duty on the market value of
properties instead of on consideration on conveyance has
General Topics 319

revolutionised the Stamp law in the State Comment?
Prior to the enactment of the Indian Stamp (Andhra Pradesh Amendment)
Act No: XXII of 1971, the stamp duty payable on the instrument of
Sales was based only on the consideration paid for the transaction. By
the AP Act No: 17 of 1986 a seperare article 47A was inserted in the
Schedule | A to the Stamp Act for levy of duty on sale deeds on the basis
of consdieration or market value of the property whichever is higher.
Though according to Sec.27, the parties must state the amount of
consideration truly and the failure to do so is an offence punishable
under Sec.64, there was large scale understatement of consideration for
the following reasons.
Firstly there is no method of ascertaining the real consideration. Black
money can easily change hands. Secondly intention to defraud
Government of revenue is a necessary condition to obtain conviction
under Sec. 64. It is very difficult for the prosecution to prove such
intention. Hence the Act was amended in 1971 (Act No.XXII of 1971)
inserting Section 47-A and prescribing duty on market value of the
property or consideration whichever is higher in respect of releases also.
It is easier to ascertain market value than the real amount of consideration.
The introduction of market value system is a necessary measure to plug
leakage of revenue. It was already tested before the Madras High Court
when the system was introduced in Madras State (now Tamilnadu) and
the High Court upheld it. It would not have done if it was a retrograde
step.

Article 46-A (Release) was substituted with effect from 16-8-1986
by a new one by Act 17 of 1986. Is there any anomaly in it and if so
discuss?

The new Article is as follows.

Art. 46-A : Any instrument (not being such a release as is provided
under Sec.23A) whereby a person renounces a claim upon another person
or against any specified property.

The anomaly is as follows : —

There is no difficulty in the implementation of this article in so far as
Release by Co-owner or Co-parcener because the Releasor has pre-existing
right for a specific share in the property which is the subject matter of the
Release. But difficulty arises in the case of Release of mortgage right,
maintenance right, indemnity right etc. Eg. ‘A’ took a loan of Rs. 1,000/- from
‘B’ and executed a deed of Mortgage offering his land worth Rs. 50,000/- as
security for repayment of the loan with interest. He repays Rs. 1,100/- to ‘B’
after one year towards loan and interest and obtains a release. The stamp duty
payable would be 3% on Rs. 50,000/- (Market Value of property over which
mortgage right is relinquished i.e., Rs. 1,500/- which is anomalous. The same
anomaly will arise in respect of Release of maintenance right, indemnity right
etc,

In order to overcome this anomulous situation the I.G., R & S directed
in his Proceedings No. S1/6569/88, dt. 11.10.1988 (and reiterated in Memo
No S2/24952/95 dated. 11-10-1995) clarified that Release of mortgage right
should be stamped with a duty of Rs. 50/- under Art. 45 “Reconveyance of
mortgaged property” which strictly speaking is applicable to mortgage
with possession.

In I.G's Proceedings No. $2/24952/95, dt. 27.9.1995 the Registering
Officers were instruscted that release of indemnity right, maintenance right,
disputed right and lease hold right should be charged to duty at 3% on the
consideration amount.

Taxation Laws should be free from uncertainty. Discuss how far
the Stamp Act conforms to this doctrine ?

Stamp duty is a tax but not fees for services rendered. It should be paid
before or at the time of execution of the document except in respect of
instruments where Stamp duty has been paid through banks under section
10A or documents stamped under Sec.31.Unlike fees it is collected
otherwise than in cash . Hence the provisions of Stamp Law should be
definite, unambiguous and easily understandable by the common man.
The Stamp Act, in its present form, hardly conforms to this doctrine.
Even the High Courts differ in the classification of documents and
assessment of the duties.

The introduction of Sec. 47-A has prolonged and still complicated matters
and confused the tax payer. The Stamp duty is payable on Market Value
of the property which is elusive. Neither the Government nor the subject
knows the real market value at any one point of time and the approximate
values fixed by the department as guidelines cannot be said as scientific
and realistic and has no legal force so as to be binding on the parties.
Sometimes the State also loses its legitamate revenue due to non-
availability of data regarding real market values of properties.

When a person receives any amount (or Cheque or Bill of exchange
or Pronote or Movable Property) exceeding Rs. 5000/- in value he
is bound to give a receipt on demand by the payer (Sec. 30). Failure
to do so is punishable with a fine upto Rs. 100/- (Sec. 65) Previously
such receipt was necessary when the amount exceeded Rs.500/-.
The amount was enhanced to Rs.5000/- with effect from 1.4.2004
(Finance Act No. 2 of 2004) (Central Act. 23 of 2004)

If an unstamped receipt is found in audit, the Audit Officer may
require a duly stamped receipt to be substituted, in its place (Sec.
34).

When an unstamped receipt is produced in evidence the court may
accept it on payment of a fine of Rs.3/- {Section 35(b)}.
Receipts cannot be certified under Sec. 32 after adjudication
(Proviso to Sec. 32)

Unstamped and insufficiently stamped receipt cannot be validated
under Sees. 41 and 42, or 40 and 42,

Such receipts should be permanently impounded and sent to the
Inspector General of Registration and Stamps, Hyderabad, who
will destroy them after 12 years from the date of execution.

Cases of fraudulant evasion of duty or willful neglect to comply
with the provisions of law should be promptly punished. Discuss.

Stamp duty is payable before or at the time of execution except in respect
14,

General Topics

of instruments where stamp duty can also be paid through Banks under
Sec.10A or documents stamped under Section 31. whether such
instruments are to be registered or not, executed or not, whether they are
to be produced in a Court or Public Office or not. Where such documents
are to be produced in a Court or Office, the scope for evasion of duty is
less. But in respect of other cases there is a tendency to evade the duty.
Parties are inclined to take the risk because the chances of detection of
evasion of duty are remote. Hence a system of penalty extending to ten
times the deficit duty is prescribed when deficitly stamed documents are
produced

The Courts have to necessarily levy penalty equal to ten times the deficit
duty and after payment of the same, the Collector can refund a part of it
under Section 45. The Collector in the case of adjudication by him can
levy a lesser penalty not exceeding 10 times the deficit duty. The Collector
should exercise the powers judiciously to curb fraudulant evasion of
duty and wilful neglect to pay the duty.

A more common method of evading duty is by under statement of
consideration or market value of property which is made punishable
under Sec. 64 read with Section 27. Such cases should be promptly
investigated and parties prosecuted to curb the tendency to evade payment
of higher duty and defraud Government.

Sec. 47-A has been introduced w.c.f. 16-8-1975 (A.P.Act XXII of 1971)
to check undervaluation of properties. But the Registering officers have
no powers to determine market values and collect duties on them. The
Revenue Officials and now the Dt. Registrars also are declared as
“Collectors” under section 47A and they should take prompt action on
the cases referred to them to evade large scale leakage of stamp ‘duties.
A failure to duly stamp a document does not affect the validity of
any contract therein contained but renders the document
inadmissible in evidence. Elucidate?

The sole object of the Act is to increase the revenues of the State though
incidentally it prevents the fabrications of antedated documents etc. The
provisions of the Act are designed to protect the State Revenues but not
to exclude evidence or to enable parties to avoid the obligations contained
in the documents on technical grounds of deficit stamp duty.
Unstamped and deficitly stamped documents can be admitted in evidence
by courts on payment of deficit duty and penalty of 10 times the deficit
duty under Sec. 35. They can also be validated under Secs. 40, 41 and
42 by collectors and then acted upon and used against the parties bound
by them.
General Topics , 327

15.

Non payment of duty at the proper time does not therefore affect the
validity of the instrument or affect the contract contained therein (vide
note 18 under section 35 APSM). It only attracts levy of penalty and the
document cannot be admitted in evidence or acted upon by an officer
unless the deficit duty and penalty are paid. The party may be allowed
time to pay such duty and penalty (vide note 18 under Sec.35 APSM -
P.52)

The party who wants the document to be admitted in evidence can pay
the deficit duty and penalty and recover them later if he is not at fault for
the deficit delay from the party who is liable to pay them under Sec. 29
(vide Sec. 44).

“A refusal to agree for compounding is ignored and acceptance of

the same is penalised”. Discuss with reference to offences under Sec.
27. Suggest remedies?
Sec. 27 says that all facts and circumstances affecting the chargeability
of an instrument to duty shall be fully and truly set forth therein. Failure
to do it with an intention to defraud Government of its revenue is
punishable with fine upto Rs. 5,000 under Sec.64 and the amount of
deficit duty under Sec. 64-A. The Collector has power to compound
offences under Sec. 70 instead of launching prosecution against the
offenders. The District Registrars and some of the Sub-Registrars, Grade-
1 and Senior Joint Sub-Registrar (Joint Sub- Registrar I) in Registrars
Offices have been invested with such power. When a case of
undervaluation is suspected, the party is given a notice so as to provide
an opportunity to get the offence compounded out of Court. The
compounding fee is usually slightly higher than the amount of total loss
(Sec.64 and 64A) caused to Government by such undervaluation together
with a penalty equal to three times the deficit duty (Section 70(2) Act
16 of 2002 with effect from 1-9-2002)
Many of the parties prefer to get the offence compounded by paying the
compounding fee. But a few are adament and do not agree for
compounding. The only alternative left is to sanction their prosecution
and proceed against them through the competent court (Sec. 71 & 72).
The fact is that very few cases succeed in court as it is difficult to prove
the intention to defraud with the result that the parties are acquitted. So
generally the Registering Officers do not go in for prosecution.

It is therefore correct to say that refusal to compound is ignored,
acceptance is penalised.
General Topics

17,

“It is tempting to evade the law and run the risk of imposition of
fine”. Elucidate with reference to Section 64?

Sec. 27 lays down that all the facts and circumstances affecting the
chargeability of an instrument to duty shall be fully and truly set forth in
the instrument. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Section
with an intention to defraud the Government is made punishable with a
fine upto Rs. 5,000 under Sec. 64 or by compounding the offence under
Sec. 70(2) levying compounding fee eqal to deficit stamp with penalty
The most common method of evading duty is by under statement of
consideration or market value of property which is made punishable
under section 64 read with Sec. 27. To curb this tendency a new section
47-A was introduced in the stamp Act with effect from 16-8-1975 (Act
No.XXII of 1971). All the Dist. Registrars are declared as “Collectors”
under Section 47-A for determining market values and collection of duties
based on them.

In economic offence such as evasion of Stamp duty emphasis to
discover intention should be less. Discuss?

Sec. 64 says that any person who with intention to defraud Government,
executes any instrument in which all the facts and circumstances affecting
the chargeability of the Instrument to wuty are not fully and truly setforth,
or being concerned with the preparation of any instrument, neglects to
set forth such facts and circumstances, or does any other act calculated
to deprive the Government of any duty or penalty under the Act is
punishable with fine which may extend to Rs. 5,000/- or with an amount
of deficit duty and penalty of three times the deficit duty under Sec. 64A
and Sec.70(2).

Depriving Government of revenue due is an economic offence. Intention
to defraud is made an essential ground for prosecution. It is necessary,
because mere non-payment of proper duty should not be a ground for
prosecution. Ignorant and innocent public may some times pay lesser
duty on documents. Ignorance or innocence must be distinguished from
mischief.

In several cases, the parties, after being informed about the deficit duty
or undervaluation may be willing to pay it with penalty. Only if they
decline to do so it should be inferred that there was an intention to commit
fraud. Intention to defraud must be a necessary ground for
prosecution though it may be difficult to prove such an intention.

What are the sailent features of partition and explain the principles
governing the determination of its Stamp duty?

(1) Stamp duty on partitions is leviable under Art. 40

(2) The duty is payable on the value of separated share or shares at
the rates prescribed in Art: 14 (Bottomry bond).

(3) To arrive at Value of Seperated Share or Shares the larger or the
largest share as the case may be should be excluded from the sum
total of the value of all the shares. If all the shares are equal one of
them should be excluded.

(4) The market value should be taken into account (vide Sec. 47-A).

(5) In respect of agricultural lands held on revenue settlement for a
period not exceeding 45 years, 25 times annual assessment may
be taken as value of the share (vide Item 85 Notification No. 13,
dated 17.12.1938)

(6) Decrees of Award, not being an award made on a reference by an
order of a court in the course of a suit, that is private awards
directing partition should be stamped as partition Sec. 2(15).

(7) Charged debts on the security of immovable property should be
deducted from the value of such immovable property. (Note 2,
page 236, A.P.S.M.).

(8) In respect of agricultural lands on revenue settlement for a period
not exceeding 45 years market value (and not 25 times the
assessment) minus charged debt or 25 times assessment whichever
is less should he taken.

(9) Movables, Cash and securities : If specifically mentioned the
value thereof should be added to the concerned share and value of
liabilities on such movable property can be deducted from the value
of the movable assets

(10) Cash paid by one sharer to another for equalisation of shares should

Explain in detail the concept of essentiality in partitions ?

Several concessions are allowed by the Act in payment of duty on

instruments of partition such as exempting the largest share from duty,

taking 25 times annual assessment as value in respect of certain

Agricultural lands, deducting charged debts from the value of property

etc. The principle underlying these concessions is that in a deed of

partition, there is no alienation of property, but only determination and
carving out the share of each co-parcener or co-owner.

The CCRA (vide B.P.No.417-R, Mis.dt.25.3.1919) ruled that certain

dispositions and provisions contained in partitions of family properties

need not be charged separately eg, provision made for marriage of minor
General Topics 331

22.

23.

sons and daughters, maintenance of parents, worship of family deitis

and maintenance of Samadhis of ancestors and the like.

Where however the provision is not essential to partition such as giving

disproportionate assets to parents and marriage of distant relatives like

nephews the clauses cannot be regarded as essential to partition but should

be charged as Settlement. (B.P.417, Mis.25.3.1919; B.P.176, Mis.

27.6.1927, B.P.45 Press 27.4.1940 - Note 12 on P. 240, APSM).

What are the precautions to be taken in writing an instrument on

an impressed stamp paper?

(1) Instrument written upon stamped paper shall be written in such a
manner that the stamp .appears on the face of the instrument and
cannot be used again or applied to any other instrument (Sec. 13).

(2) No second instrument chargeable with duty shall be written on a
stamp paper on which an instrument chargeable with duty was
already written. (Sec. 14). .

(3) Stamp specifically prescribed for a particular class of document
should not be used for other documents. {Rule 3(ii)}.

(4) Stamps purchased in A.P. alone should be used for execution of
documents chargeable with duty in A.P. State {Rule 3(iii)}.

(5) Stamps purchased for the use of a particular person cannot be used
by or for the use of any other person. {Rule 6(2)}.

(6) When two or more sheets are used for a document a portion of the
document should appear on each sheet. {Rule 7(i)}.

(7) When stamps are not sufficient for the document it can be continued
on white paper but a substantial part of the document should appear
on the stamp paper {Rule 7(2)}.

What are the conditions necessary for execution of an agreement

relating to deposit of title deeds?

(1) Agreement relating to deposit of title deeds applies only to certain
towns notified under Sec. 58(f) of T.P. Act 1882. But so far as the
stamp duty is concerned, this aspect need not be taken into
consideration. The place of deposit is criteria.

(2) The mortgage deed creates a right in the property itself while
Agreement relating to deposit of title deeds creates a security on
the title deeds. Hence words indicating creation of right in property
should be avoided.

(3) The document should contain only the bargain relating to deposit of
title deeds and matters ancillary to it. If it contains all conditions
normally found in mortgage deeds, it should be treated as a

What are the implications of Sec. 35?

The Section deals with unstamped and insufficiently stamped documents
produced in evidence in Courts. The Court shall impound such documents
and levy the deficit duty and penalty equal to ten times the deficit duty.
If the party pays them, the Court will admit it in evidence and send an
authenticated copy of it to the Collector who can refund a part of the
penalty if he thinks fit {Sec. 38(1) and 39}.

If the party fails to pay them the court will reject the document in evidence
27

General Topics 333

and should send the original to the Collector {Sec. 38(2)} who will levy
deficit duty and penalty not exceeding ten times the deficit duty (Sec.
40).

The party who is not bound to pay under Section 29 but paying the duty
and the penalty levied by the court can recover the same from the person
who is liable to pay them under Section 29. (Vide Section 44).

Unstamped receipts can be admitted in evidence on payment of a fine of
Rs. 3/- This section does not apply to criminal proceedings and to
documents executed by or in favour of Government and to documents
certified by Collectors under Sec, 32.(Sec.35(b)).

What are the instruments the rates of stamp duty on which can be
prescribed by Government of India alone. Discuss the necessity for
such porovision.

Government of India alone are competent to prescribe the rates of duty
on the instruments listed out at entry 91 in List-I to the 7th Schedule to
the Constitution. They are :—

1. Bill of Exchange
Cheques
Promissory Note
Bill of Lading
Letter of Credit
Policy of Insurances
Transfer of Share
Debentures

Proxy

10. Receipt

Duties payable on the above instruments are payable as prescribed against
concerned Article in Schedule -1. The instruments are generally used in
the course of trade and commerce and have all India circulation. If
different State Governments prescribe different rates for them there will
be great hardship to the public in paying the difference in duty every
time they are received in other states. Hence the power was vested in
Government of India.

Explain the purpose, effectiveness and. efficacy of such rule?

CONAN AYWDN
334

29,

General Topics
For various reasons like shortgage of paper and printing material etc.,
the central Stamp store, Nasik would at times, be unlable to meet the
demand for supply of stamps. Unscrupulous persons are prone to seize
such opportunity to corner the stocks-by purchasing them in the names
of fictitious persons and then selling them at a premium. The licensed
Stamp Vendors also may write-some names in their endorsements on
stamps as though they were sold out and then sell them at a higher price.
They thus make the supply position worse and indulge in malpractice to
the detriment of the public. Hence Rule 6(2) was introduced to prevent
such malpractices. (vide G.O.Ms.No.340 Rev. dt.15.4.1967) Rule 6(2)
enforces that the person for whose use the stamp paper was purchased
or his agent, or representative alone should use it and none elsé. Hence
the scope to corner stock is largely eliminated. Further if the Stamps
purchased by others are allowed to be used by persons other than the
persons for whom they were purchased there is scope for execution of
antedated documents and increase of litigation. This is eliminated under
Rule 6(2).

What are the steps taken by Government to prevent creation of

The following steps were taken to prevent artificial scarcity of Stamps.

(1) Stamp counters were opened in almost all Registration offices for
sale of Stamps of all descriptions direct to public on tendering
cash.

(2) The Sub-Registrars who are ex-officio Vendors are declared as “

Rule 9. vide G.O.Ms.No.340 Rev. dt.15.4.1967

(3) Stamp Rule 6(2) was introduced prescribing that Stamps

of documents to be stamped with special adhesive labels though

withdrawn from circulation from |.4.1959 were reintro-duced after
being over printed. (Vide Rule 2-A of Rules for supply and
distribution of Stamps introduced in October 1967).

Elucidate with three examples in each case the object and Scope of
Sections 4, 5 and 6 of the Act?
Section - 4 : The Section deals with cases where several instruments are
employed to complete a single transaction. It applies to sales, mortgages
and settlements alone. When more than one instrument is employed to
complete a single transaction i.e sales, mortgages and settlements, the
full duty should be paid on the principal deed and the others can be
stamped with only Rs. 5/- each. The object of this Section is to avoid
double taxation. The object of the Act is to tax the instruments but not
the transaction. Here, a deviation is made and transaction is taken as
criterion.

Examples :

(1) ‘A’ sells a house on his behalf and on behalf of his minor Son ‘B’.
‘B’ ratifies the sale on attaining majority. The ratification deed
falls under Sec. 4.
General Topics 337

34,

 

(2) ‘A’ sellsa land to ‘B’ through a sale deed. ‘C’ the undivided brother
ratifies the sale. It falls under Sec. 4.

(3) ‘A’ settles the property on ‘B’. ‘B’ through a separate deed
accepts the gift. The laterdocument falls under Sec. 4. (See
also notes | to 3 under Sec. 4.Page 22 APSM)

Section - 5 : If a single document embodies several distinct matters it

attracts the aggregate of the duties payable on each such matter. The

object of the section is to safeguard Government revenue. It is the number
of transactions that count but not the instrument employed.

Examples :

(1) Many ryots holding different Pattas executed a General Power of
Attorney in favour of ‘A’. Sec. 5 applies. (Note 4 on P. 245, APSM).

(2) A purchaser, at an auction, purchases several lots. Only one
instrument is executed. Sec. 5 applies (Vide Note 8, under Sec. 5
Page 23 APSM).

(3) ‘A’ settles his house on ‘B’, his wife, for life and thereafter to
revert to her brother. The document is a settlement for life and
Gift falling under Sec. 5 as it relates to two distinct matters

Section - 6: If an instrument falls under two or more descriptions
under Schedule | or 1A as the case may be and where the duties
payable on each such description differs is chargeable only with the
highest of such duties. It is intended to avoid double taxation as also
ambiguity in payment of duties on documents falling under several
descriptions.

Examples :

(1) ‘A’ sells his house to ‘B! and offers his land as indemnity against
loss if any caused to ‘B’ due to any defect in title. Sec.6
applies.(Note 4, under Sec. 6 Page 26 APSM).

(2) ‘A’ executes alease in favour of ‘B’ and offers his own property
as security for prompt payment of the rent. Sec. 6 applies. (Notes
1 and 2 under Sec. 6 Page 25 APSM).

(3) A company in consideration of money advanced by a.Bank,
executes a Trust. in favour of the Bank. The document is chargeable
with higher duty as amortgage. (Vide Note 3 under Sec. 6 Page
25 APSM ).

“A simple dedication of property to an idol though one for religious

purpose, is only a Gift and not a settlement’. Elucidate.

The Calcutta High Court in 1936 (AIR 1936, Cal. 556) and the Nagpore

High Court in 1944 (AIR 1944, Nag. 33) ruled that a deed conveying

property in favour of certain deities was not settlement but gift. The

reasons advanced were that the word settlement refers to a disposition
of successive interests in immovable properties generally couched in
the form of a trust. It is difficult to say that where a gift is made to a deity
the deity is to be regarded as a trustee. The definition in specific Relief
Act was relied upon. But subsequently in 1951 (AIR 1955, NUC (Cal.)
820 the Calcutta Hivh Court ruled that a deed by which the property of
General Topics 339

37.

the executant was given to dietees is a settlement deed for the purpose

of Stamp Act though there is no trust or disposition of successive interests.

Such docts are now clarified as Gift (Settlements that is gift for registration

purpose and settlement for stamp purpose) (Vide I.G.’s Proceedings No.

$1/4899-A/89, dt. 14.7.1994.) See Item 12 under “Gift” in Chapter 8.

Though a Collector under Sec. 48, a District Registrar rarely

exercises this power himself. Why?

Sec. 48 empowers the Collector to collect all duties and penalties etc.,

under the Act by distress and sale of movable property of any person

from whom the same are due or by any other process in force for the
recovery of arrears of land revenue.

The District Registrars are declared as Collectors under Sec. 48. (Vide
General Topic:

39.

40.

41.

Note 2(4) under Sec. 2(9) APSM). But the District Registrars have no
machinery to exercise this power and they are not invested with any
powers under the Revenue Recovery Act. Hence they rarely exercise
this power. They address the regular Revenue authorities whenever it
becomes necessary to recover the deficit duties, penalties and
compounding fees etc.

Enumerate the powers of Govt. with reference to Sec. 9 of the
Stamp Act?
Sec. 9 empowers the Government to reduce or remit prospectively or
retrospectively the duties payable on any instrument or class of
instruments. It also empowers the Government to provide for composition
or consolidation of duties in case of issue of debentures etc., by Corporate
Bodies.
Government means — (1) In respect of documents mentioned in entry
91 List-l, 7th Schedule to constitution, Central Government and (2) in
respect of other instruments, State Government.
How is a document evidencing adoption and containing disposition
of property assessed to stamp duty?
If a document merely records the fact of udoption and the legal effect of
such adoption such as the adopted son acquiring right in the property as
anatural son, the document is chargeable only as deed of adoption under
Article 3, Schedule I-A.
Narrate the social and rescue provisions of chargeability reliefs
and remissions in Stamp Law for the benefit of various sections
of public?
Unlike registration fee, which is a charge for services rendered, stamp
duty is a tax which has no relevance to services rendered by the state to
the tax payer
India is a Socialistic country whose aim is to tax the rich and help the
poor. In pursuance of this policy, the legislature incorporated certain
exemptions in the Schedule to the Stamp Act itself and the Executive

Distinguish between impounding under Section 33 and references

under Sec.47-A under the Stamp Act, explaining the procedural

differences ?

Section 33(1)

(i) When a deficitly stamped document is produced before a public
officer, the document will be impounded under Sec. 33 and sent to
the Collector under Sec. 38(2). The Collector provisionally
determines the duty and issues a notice to the concerned parties.
After receipt of the replies he issues a final order determining the
deficit duty and levies penalty not exceeding ten times the deficit
duty under Sec. 40. On payment of the same he adds a certificate
of such payment under Sec. 42. The deficitly stamped document
cannot be registered unless the certificate is added under Sec. 42.

(ii) If the party declares the higher value in the document but does not
pay the duty on it, the document can be impounded and the
procedure under Sec. 33, 38 and 40 and 42 followed.

Section 47A : When, in the case of Sale, Gift. Exchange, Release or

Partition, the Registering officer feels that the market value of the property

is not setforth as per the Basic Value Guideline Registers, he withholds

it from registering. He then sends a reference to the Collector under Sec.

47-A for determination of the value and collection of the deficit duty.
General Topics 343

43.

The Collector issues a notice to the parties concerned and after taking
into consideration the grounds and the points mentioned in the Indian
Stamp (Prevention of under valuation Rules 1975) finally determines the
value and calls upon the parties to pay the deficit duty under intimation to
the Registering Officer. The party can pay the same or go in appeal to
the Civil Court.(Sub sections (4) and (5) under Section 47-A)
Enumerate the details that a speakding order shall contain in a case
of adjudication and revision under the Stamp Act and Why?
When an insufficiently stamped instrument is impounded by the Collector
or received by him, he provisionally determines the duty and issues a
notice to the concerned parties. After the receipt of their replies, he issues
the final order determining the deficit duty and penalty under Sec. 40.
This order shall be a speaking order containing the following particulars.
(1) The recitals in the document.
(2) The stamp duty if any borne by the document.
(3) The Stamp Duty required as per the provisional determination by
the Collector with the authority namely provisions of Stamp
Act and Schedule.
(4) The names of parties to whom the notices were issued and the
mode of service.
(5) Details of representations received from the parties and the
grounds advanced therein.

(6) Whether they are accepted or rejected and the reasons therefor.
(7) Final order determining the deficit duty.

(8) _ of penalty. If maximum penalty equal to ten times the deficit duty
is levied the reasons therefor.

If the party is aggrieved by the order of the Collector he may apply to the
C.C.R.A. for revision under Sec. 56. The C.C.R.A. after examining the
records, and taking into consideration, the grounds of appeal, issues an
order allowing or rejecting the appeal. The said order shall be speaking
order containing the following particulars.

(1) The case of applicant.

(2) The grounds advanced in the revision petition.

(3) Reasons for accepting or rejecting the grounds.

(4) Final order.

The speaking order must contain all these particulars to apprise the parties
344

44,

45,

46.

47.

General Topics
of the reasons for demanding the deficit duty and penalty and to enable
him to prefer further appeal if he so desires.

Enumerate the Dos and Don’ts in operating Franking Machines?

Dos : Check if the seal is in tact, machine is unlocked, denominations
are in xerox position, there is sufficient ink in the ink well, date in the
machine is set, place the handle in 6’O Clock position,

Don’ts : The handle should never be rotated anti-clock wise. Do not
rotate the handle unless it is required for franking purpose (GSO Memo
2/21659/95, dt. 6.12.1995).

Is Penalty leviable on deficitly stamped instruments detected in Audit
under Sec, 73? What are consequences?

Penalty is not leviable on deficitly stamped instrument detected in Audit
under Sec. 73 (Rule 3 of the Rules for the collection of duties - Chapter
1H)

Editors Submission : It does not appear to be a wise step because parties
will have no hesitation in executing unregistered documents on stamps
of nominal value as they can pay the deficit duty without any penalty if
and when they are detected in Audit. Compulsiry levy of penalty acts as
a deterrent against evasion of Stamp Duty.

What are the reasons that compelled the Govt. to introduce Art.
42(g) in Sch. I-A to the Indian Stamp Act?

General Power of Attorney : General Power of Attorney authorising
the Agent to act in the name and on behalf of the Principal (owner of
General Topics 345

48.

49,

property) in all offices was very popular with the registering public. It
enabled the Real Estate Dealer to purchase land in bulk, obtain General
Power of Attorney on Rs. 50/- on Non-Judicial Stamps from the owner
and sell the land in bits executing the sale deeds on behalf of the Principal.
In this way the payment of stamp duty twice was avoided. In some cases
where the transfer was not legally permissible as in the case of assigned
lands and lands affected by ceiling laws the landlords gave General
Powers of Attorney to the purchasers assuring them that they would
serve as title deeds. Innocent public believed them. Gram Panchayats,
Municipalities and even Municipal Corporation gave building permits
in the name of Attorneys and/or assessed Tax in their names though the
Attorneys are not real owners of the land. In this way Government are
put to loss of Stamp Revenue due on market value of the property and
local bodies also lost transfer duty due to them. It has given scope for
unnessary litigation also.

In order to check the loss of revenue, Government of Andhra Pradesh
amended the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 by A.P. Amendment Act, 21 of
1995 by introducing Article 42(g) in Schedule I-A. Prescribing Stamp
duty at 5% on the value of the property in respect of which the Attorney
was given power to sell or otherwise transfer any immovable property.
This act came into force w.e.f. 1.4.1995.

What are the adverse effects felt by a Section of the Public by Art
42(g)?

This measure has hit some genuine parties who reside out of India or out
of Andhra Pradesh or at distant places in A.P. and own property solely
or jointly with family members in Andnra Pradesh. When they execute
the Power of Attorney authorising their kith and kin in Andhra Pradesh
to sell the property they are made to pay 5% duty on the market value of
the property in addition to about 10 per cent towards registration expenses
on sale deed. Persons living abroad or in for-away places in India
cannot afford to come to Andhra Pradesh for the sake of registration of
the sale deed nor can they afford to pay stamp duty at advalorem rates
on GPA on the market value of the property.

What is the alternative that can be legally adopted to avoid heavy
stamp duty under Art.42 (g) of Sch. I-A?

The following alternative can be conveniently adopted available in the
Registration Act and Indian Stamp Act.

Power of Attorney are of two kinds:

(1) General Power of Attorney i.e. Power authorising the Agent to
execute documents in the name and on behalf of the Principal.
346

General Topics

50.

(2) Special Power of Attorney i.e. Power authorising the Agent to
procure registration of document executed or signed by the
Principal.

The former category of General Powers of Attorney are attracted
by Art. 42(g) requiring stamp duty at advalorem rates In the latter
case (Special Power of Attorney) the power should be attested in
the manner laid down in Sec. 33 of the Registration Act.1908 and
requires a stamp duty of Rs. 20/- only under Art. 42(a).
What is the procedure for Stamping a sale deed executed out of
India and later received in Andhra Pradesh?

If the Principal is residing abroad, the sale deed and special power of
attorney drawn-up on unstamped papers can be sent to him with a request
to execute (sign) the sale deed and get it attested by 2 local witnesses.
Thereafter he should take the Power of Attorney to the Notary Public or
Indian Consul or Vice Consul and sign before him and get it attested by
him. He should send both the documents to the Agent in Andhra Pradesh
who should, within 3 months from date of their receipt, present them to
the concerned district Registrar along with a certificate from the
concerned Sub-Registrar on the Market value of the property described
in the sale deed with a request for stamping them under Sec. 18 of the
Stamp Act. The District Registrar will collect the amount in cash and
get the special Adhesive labels of the required value affixed on the sale
deed and Rs. 20/- on the Power of Attorney affixed by the Joint Sub-
Registrar (Proper Officer) and return the documents immediately to the
Agent, adding a certificate that it was stamped under Sec. 18. Thereafter,
the agent may present the sale deed alongwith the special Power of
Attorney to the Sub-Registrar concerned for the registration of Sale Deed.

NOTE: The C & IGRS in his circular memo No.S5/5565/97 dt 24-9-1997

51.

clarified that the stamps purchased in Andhra Pradesh relating to property
situated in Andhra Pradesh though executed outside India are still
valid irrespective of its place of its execution.

What is the procedure in respect of sale deeds executed out of Andhra
Pradesh in India and received in Andhra Pradesh ?

Stamp duty on such documents consists of duty payable under Indian
Stamp Act and the transfer duty payable under the relevant local bodies
act. The said local bodies Acts do not apply to other states, for example
if a document relating to sale of a house in Srikakulam is executed in
Bhuvaneswar (Orissa State) the duty payable thereon is only at the rate
prescribed for conveyance. Transfer duty is not chargeable in orissa state
as A.P. Municipalities Act does not apply there. However on receipt of
Stamp Duties on documents (Illustrations) 347

N.B:

ii)

iii)
iv)
v)

vi)
vi)

the document in Srikakulam the difference of duty if any for the sale and
full transfer duty should be paid, in the same way as a document received
from a foreign country. (Sec. 18). .

However in respect of documents relating to properties in A.P. executed
in Tamil Nadu and vice-versa the Transfer duty also should be paid in
the state where the document is executed as there is reciprocal
arrangement between the states to adjust the Transfer duty, through the
respective Accountants General

24. A prospecting licence granted by Government to an individual for

Such document should be stamped as an agreement under Art. 6(A),
Sch I-A. The security deposit of cash need not be separately charged as
mortgage with or without possession in view of the ruling of the Supreme
Court in Forest lease case in which it was held that money is not a

25. In an instrument between forest department and a Contractor it

was recited that in respect of a bamboo coupe the contractor was to
be allowed to fell and remove bamboos for a period of 5 years for a
rent of Rs. 5,000/- P.A. The contractor had deposited an amount of
Rs. 5,000/- in cash as security for due performance of the terms and
it was to be adjusted towards rent of last year.
The document is only an agreement if the bamboos are in grown up
stage and that the period of 5 years is allowed to cut and remove them.
Deposit of cash need not be charged additionally as mortgage with or
without possession as it is not a specified property. So the document is
only an agreement. (Item 19 of Page 180 of A.P.S.M.). If they are in
growing stage it amounts to a lease.

26. ‘A’ has taken a loan of Rs.5,000/- from a Bank and deposited the

Title deeds of property as security. The loan has to be discharged in
certain monthly instalments. It is also agreed that in case of default
in payment, the Bank is empowered on behalf of ‘A’ to sell away
property and adjust towards cost.
According to Note 4 under Art. 6, Schedule I on P.80- of A.P. Stamp
Manual 1974, the document has to be classified as an Agreement relating
to deposit of Title deeds chargeable under Art.7, Sch I-A. But according
to Note 38 under Art. 40, Sch I on P.126 of the A.P Stamp Manual, the
power of sale created an interest in immovable property and is therefore
chargeable as a mortgage under Art, 35(b) of Sch. I-A. It is advisable to
follow the latter decision.

PARI PASSU AGREEMENT and what is the stamp payable
thereon?

An industrialist or a firm or a company obtains credit facilities from
various financial institutions by offering all or any of the following
security that is on one and the same security -

a. Simple mortgage of the lands and buildings.

b. Deposit of Title deeds

c. Hypothecation of movable properties.

‘When the borrower takes loans from more than one financial institution,
the subsequent creditors insist that their rights in the mortgaged properties
shall rank PARIPASSU (on par ) with the earlier creditors. Thus the
mortgagor and the mortgagees enter into an agreement bringing all the
creditors on par, so far as their mortgage rights are concerned. Such
agreement is called PARI PASSU agreement chargable under Art 6(C)
with a stamp of Rs. 100/- (IG's progs No.S2/24846/82 dt 15-10-1982)
Agreement for sale of Agricultural property

An agreement for sale of AGRICULTURAL LANDS is not covered by
Article 6(B) of Schedule 1A. Such agreements fall under Art. 6(A) only
(A.P. High Court Judgment dt. 7-9-2004 in CRP No. 6053 of 2002 C &
IGRS Memo No.S1/16160/04 dt. 2-3-2005

Agreement for sale of Vacant Site

Agrement for sale of VACANT SITE falls under the general article 6-A
of Schedule 1A but not under Article 6(B) (A.P. High Court Judgement
dt. 8-11-2003 in CRP No. 4396 of 2003 - 2004(1) ALD 557)
Agreement of sale cum GPA

When an agreement of Sale cum general power of attorney is given in
favour of a person it can be construed that possession of the Schedule
property is delivered and the words evidencing delivery of possession
employed in the instrument are redundant, auxillary, and no
preponderence need be given to such words (CCRA & C and IGRS progs
No. CCRA-1/13754/2005 dt 17-02-2006)

Agreement relating to deposit of tittle deeds (Equitable Mortgage)

Explain its chargeability to stamp duty ?

(i) | Anagreement “evidencing an agreement to secure the payment of
a loan upon the deposit of title deeds" was held to be a mortgage
deed as it created a "right over property’ viz. the right to bring the
specified property to sale for the satisfaction of the claim. (AIR
1939 RC 167). The Stamp Act makes no difference between a
legal mortgage and an equitable mortgage. If a document falls
within the special class of documents referred to in Art.7 of
Schedule 1A of Stamp Act then it would be charged as an agreement
relating to the deposit of title deeds and not as mortgage deed.
(Vide commentary on section 2 (17) (Mortgage deed) of the Indian
Stamp Act by K.Krishnamurthy Sth edition - Page87/6th edition
page 82)
Stamp Duties on documents (Illustrations) 357

42,

43.

(ii) A confirmatory letter given by the mortgagor to the mortgagee
referring to the previous execution of a pronote and deposit of
titledeeds by way of equitable mortgage as security for the
repayment of the loan and setting out in the schedule appended to
it the title deeds so deposited on a particular date and indicating
confirmation of the party of his intention to create equitable
mortgage on subsequent date granting loans after recording the
facts in a register. The letter is not a subsequent or a follow up to
any proviously executed (duly stamped) document and hence the -
letter has to be treated as "Agreement relating to deposit of title
deeds” chargeable under article 7 of Schedule-1A. (Memo No.
$1/21544/87 dated 4-4-1988 of the IGR &S)
